subject: Science
title: Periodic Table
learningOutcomes: State what the periodic table is and how elements are arranged by atomic number.
Define atomic number and write the electron arrangement of the first 18 elements.
Explain what periods and groups are, and how atomic number and reactivity change across them.
Describe Groups I–VIII — alkali metals, halogens and noble gases — and their reactivity trends.
Describe the properties and uses of metals, non-metals and metalloids.

sections.heading: The Periodic Table & Atomic Number
sections.body: The periodic table is a system for arranging all the chemical elements. Elements are listed in order of increasing atomic number — the number of protons in the atom. The arrangement also shows how the electrons are shared among the shells: up to 2 in the first shell, up to 8 in the second, and up to 8 (stable) in the third.

sections.heading: Periods and Groups
sections.body: A period is a horizontal row; across a period the atomic number increases and the element at the left has 1 outer electron (very reactive) while the element at the right has a full shell (unreactive). A group is a vertical column; all its elements have the same number of outer-shell electrons, so they behave similarly. Groups are numbered by the number of outer electrons.

sections.heading: The Element Families
sections.body: Group I are the alkali metals (1 outer electron, very reactive, reactivity increases down). Group II are the alkaline earth metals (2 outer electrons). Group VII are the halogens (7 outer electrons, reactive, coloured, poisonous; reactivity decreases down). Group VIII/0 are the noble gases, which are unreactive because their outer shells are full.

sections.heading: Metals, Non-metals & Metalloids
sections.body: A stepped line divides the metals (left) from the non-metals (right). Metals are shiny, malleable, ductile, sonorous, good conductors and strong. Silicon, on the line, is a metalloid. Useful metals include lead (malleable, roofs), tungsten (glows, light bulbs), copper (wires), aluminium (heat, saucepans; light, cables), iron and steel (strong, engines and bridges) and brass (sonorous, instruments).

definitions.definition: The number of protons in an atom; it fixes the element’s place in the table.
A horizontal row of the periodic table.
A vertical column; its elements have the same number of outer-shell electrons.
Group I — very reactive metals with one outer electron.
Group VII — reactive, coloured, poisonous non-metals with seven outer electrons.
Group VIII/0 — unreactive gases with full outer shells.
An element such as silicon with some metal and some non-metal properties.
Able to be hammered or bent into shape.
Able to be pulled into wires.
Making a ringing sound when hit.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (e.g. steel, brass, solder).

examTips: To write an electron arrangement, fill the shells inside-out: 2, then 8, then 8. Sulphur (16) → 2,8,6.
Group number = number of outer-shell electrons. Reactivity increases DOWN the metal groups (I, II) but DOWN the halogens it decreases (top is most reactive).
Atomic number = protons only. Protons + neutrons = mass number.

interactiveLesson.instructions: Explore the key regions of the periodic table. Select every hotspot to continue.

hotspots.label: Group I — Alkali Metals
hotspots.fact: The far-left column. One outer electron, very reactive; reactivity increases down the group.

hotspots.label: Group VII — Halogens
hotspots.fact: Near the right. Seven outer electrons (one empty space), reactive, coloured and poisonous.

hotspots.label: Group VIII/0 — Noble Gases
hotspots.fact: The last column. Full outer shells make them stable and unreactive.

hotspots.label: Metal / Non-metal Line
hotspots.fact: A stepped line divides metals (left) from non-metals (right). Silicon on the line is a metalloid.

hotspots.label: A Period (Row)
hotspots.fact: Across a period the atomic number increases; the left element is very reactive, the right has a full shell.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is the atomic number of an element?

options: The number of protons in an atom
The number of protons plus electrons

practiceQuestions.explanation: The atomic number is the number of protons.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is the electron arrangement of sulphur?
A period in the periodic table is a…
practiceQuestions.explanation: A period is a horizontal row.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Elements in the same group have the same number of…
practiceQuestions.explanation: A group shares the same number of outer electrons.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is the name of Group I?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Group I is the alkali metals.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why are halogens (Group VII) very reactive?

options: Their atoms have one empty space in the outer shell

practiceQuestions.explanation: Seven outer electrons means one empty space, so they react easily.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why do noble gases not react?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Full outer shells make noble gases stable.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The atomic number is the number of protons plus electrons.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False — atomic number is protons only.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Reactivity of the halogens increases down the group.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False — it decreases down; the top is most reactive.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Brass is a sonorous alloy used for musical instruments.
A stepped ______ divides metals from non-metals.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The stepped line separates metals and non-metals.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A metal that can be pulled into wires is ______.
Why is silicon called a metalloid?

options: It has some metal and some non-metal properties

practiceQuestions.explanation: Metalloids share properties of metals and non-metals.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The third shell can hold up to 18 electrons but is stable at…
practiceQuestions.explanation: 8 outer electrons give a stable arrangement.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why is lead a good material for roofs?

options: It is malleable, so it can be shaped

practiceQuestions.explanation: Lead is malleable and can be shaped to waterproof roofs.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange these Period 3 elements from left to right (increasing atomic number):
sequencingActivity.explanation: Across Period 3 the atomic number increases: Na 11, Mg 12, Al 13, Si 14.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Element X is at the far-left of Period 4 and element Y is a noble gas. Which statement is correct?

options: X has 1 outer electron and is very reactive; Y has a full shell and is unreactive
Both X and Y are unreactive
X is a noble gas and Y is an alkali metal

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: The left of a period = 1 outer electron (very reactive); noble gases have full shells (unreactive).

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Sodium is above potassium in Group I; fluorine is above chlorine in Group VII. Which is true about reactivity?

options: Sodium is more reactive than potassium
Chlorine is more reactive than fluorine
Potassium is more reactive than sodium, but fluorine is more reactive than chlorine

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Metals get more reactive DOWN the group; halogens get LESS reactive down (top is most reactive).

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: An atom has the arrangement 2,8,7. Which group is it in and how will it behave?

options: Group II — has two outer electrons
Group VIII/0 — an unreactive noble gas
Group VII (a halogen) — very reactive, needs one more electron

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: 2,8,7 has 7 outer electrons → Group VII halogen, one space short of a full shell, so very reactive.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Solder (a tin–lead alloy) melts before either pure tin or pure lead. Why?

options: Solder is not really a metal
Tin and lead do not melt at all
Mixing the metals disturbs the regular atom arrangement, lowering the melting point
Alloys always have higher melting points

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Alloying disturbs the atoms’ regular arrangement, so an alloy often melts below its pure metals.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A student says "the atomic number is protons + electrons, and reactivity increases down every group." What is wrong?

options: Only the first part is wrong
Only the second part is wrong
Both parts are wrong: atomic number is protons only, and halogens get LESS reactive down the group

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Atomic number = protons only; and the halogens are more reactive at the top, not the bottom.
